messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At forty-one, Phan used to move through space the way other people breathe—effortlessly, intuitively, as if his body were a language all its own. He had been a dancer since he was a boy in Vietnam, and then professionally for two decades in the United States. But that was before the aid convoy. Before the six months he spent as a relief worker in a contested region of the Middle East, distributing medical supplies to villages that had been shelled and re-shelled until they were hardly more than rubble. He had gone because he believed in something—in the idea that a person could stand between violence and the vulnerable and make a difference. He had not anticipated the morning when a mortar struck the warehouse where he and three others were loading trucks. He had not anticipated the fire, the screams, the way the air turned thick and chemical. He had not anticipated that he would be the one who ran.

Phan had been standing near the rear bay door when the first explosion tore through the front of the building. The heat wave knocked him flat. For a moment, everything was dust and ringing, and then he saw the flames spreading fast, crawling up pallets of bandages and bottled water. He heard a colleague—a woman named Samira—calling for help from somewhere near the office. He remembered the layout. He remembered that the rear exit was twenty feet behind him. He also remembered that he did not go toward her voice. He turned and ran. By the time the fire crews arrived, Samira was dead. The official report said she had been trapped by falling debris. Phan knew only that he had not tried to find her. He had not even looked back.

In the months that followed, that moment replayed itself in his mind not as a memory but as a recurring, uninvited present. He would be standing at the kitchen counter, reaching for a glass, and suddenly he was back in the warehouse—the heat on his skin, the acrid smell of burning plastic and insulation flooding his nostrils. The smell of anything burnt, even toast, could trigger it. So could the smell of alcohol, because there had been a spilled bottle of medical sanitizer near the exit, its sharp odor mixing with the smoke. And so could the time of day: late morning, around 10:45, when the mortar had hit. He learned to dread that hour. He learned to keep the windows closed, to avoid cooking, to ask his wife not to pour wine in his presence. He never explained why.

What frightened Phan most was not the memory itself but what the memory told him about who he was. He had believed himself to be a good person, someone who would act bravely in a crisis. His flight from the warehouse had violated that belief so thoroughly that he could no longer trust his own character. He was certain that his reaction proved he was a lousy coper—weak, selfish, fundamentally unreliable. He began to notice this failure everywhere. When he felt his heart race at the smell of smoke, he told himself that other people would have handled it calmly. When he could not bring himself to rehearse with his dance company because the studio’s heating system sometimes emitted a faint burnt odor, he concluded that he could not rely on himself to function in any demanding situation. He stopped taking lead roles. He stopped taking any roles that required improvisation, because improvisation demanded a trust in his own instincts that he no longer possessed. His agent called it a creative block. Phan knew it was something worse.

The consequences accumulated quietly. His wife, Mei, began to notice that he flinched when she hugged him unexpectedly. He stopped going to the grocery store because the cleaning aisle smelled of bleach, which reminded him of the sanitizer. He stopped attending family dinners at his in-laws’ house because someone always lit candles. He told Mei he was tired, overworked, that the company was demanding too much. She believed him at first. But after a year of this, she had grown frustrated and hurt. She did not know about Samira. He had never told her. He could not bear to speak the words aloud, because speaking them would mean admitting, in a permanent way, that he was the kind of man who ran.

What finally brought Phan to seek help was a single moment in the dance studio. He was warming up alone, trying to stretch his hamstrings, when the building’s furnace kicked on and a faint burnt smell drifted through the vents. He was on the floor in seconds, his body rigid, his mind back in the warehouse, his hands pressed against the wooden floorboards as if he were trying to push himself upright and run again. When it passed, he lay there for a long time, staring at the ceiling. He was afraid that if he did not change something, he would lose Mei, lose his career, lose whatever was left of the life he had built. But what he hoped for, more than anything, was to one day believe that he was not defined by the worst moment of his life.
